This asymmetric, unexplained treatment of two structurally identical nodes is an internal inconsistency in what the revision wrote.

control.balance_loop's rev-29 write adds torque_limit and a new constrains edge to electrical.driver_left and electrical.driver_right; electrical.battery_pack's rev-33 write adds continuous_motor_current_draw/continuous_motor_power_draw, constraining the same two drivers. electrical.driver_right (rev 32) received a follow-up (two new quantities). electrical.driver_left (worktree/design/nodes/electrical.driver_left.json, rev 31) was rewritten with the exact same quantities as its prior revision (rev 13) and carries no no_change_justified entry. A changed quantity in two upstream nodes did not reach a node it constrains, with no follow-up change and no stated reason -- a [rule] violation, explicitly not excused by the Unwritten-records rule, which names [rule]'s own follow-up/justification requirement as an exception to it.

firmware.fall_detector (design/nodes/firmware.fall_detector.json, rev 29) names electrical.imu in its 'constrains' list, a new obligation under cross-domain standards §5. electrical.imu's rewrite (design/nodes/electrical.imu.json, rev 30) is byte-identical in its quantities to the prior revision (rev 17) and carries no no_change_justified field addressing firmware.fall_detector at all. The no_change_justified prose the revision did write -- on electrical.control_board (rev 31) and control.balance_loop (rev 32), both keyed 'electrical.imu' -- addresses a change to electrical.imu's own quantities that never happened (they are unchanged), leaving the actual new obligation (from fall_detector to electrical.imu) unaddressed. This is an inconsistency between the revision's own propagation mechanism and what it actually wrote. Secondarily, firmware.fall_detector's 13 Hz sample_rate (sourced as 'the lowest LSM6DS33 output data rate') does not match the real part's documented ODR ladder (lowest = 12.5 Hz) and cannot be checked against parts_sheet.json, whose R8.09/R8.10 ODR rows are null, which is a further, lower-confidence inconsistency between the written value and its own stated source.

firmware.fall_detector (design/nodes/firmware.fall_detector.json, rev 29, a wholly new node and therefore a changed quantity by construction) names electrical.imu in its 'constrains' list. Per cross-domain standards §5, electrical.imu's owning role therefore owes either a later change to electrical.imu or a non-empty no_change_justified reason recorded on electrical.imu itself. electrical.imu's rewrite (design/nodes/electrical.imu.json, rev 30, version 2) is byte-identical in every quantity to its prior revision (rev 17, version 1) and carries no no_change_justified field at all -- neither a real follow-up nor a stated reason. The no_change_justified prose the revision did write is instead attached to electrical.control_board (rev 31) and control.balance_loop (rev 32), both keyed 'electrical.imu', which addresses whether those two downstream nodes need to respond to a change in electrical.imu -- a change that, per the identical content, never occurred, so that obligation did not even exist. The actual obligation created by firmware.fall_detector's new edge to electrical.imu is therefore left silently unaddressed, exactly what cross-domain standards §5 says must 'never [be] silently passed'.

The revision's own written record is internally inconsistent. electrical.control_board (design/journal.jsonl rev 29; design/nodes/electrical.control_board.json) adds board_length, board_width and board_thickness and newly lists mechanical.chassis among the nodes it constrains. electrical.regulator_5v's parallel follow-up is satisfied by a specific no_change_justified entry (rev 30). electrical.control_board's new board_length/board_width/board_thickness quantities (journal rev 29) newly add mechanical.chassis to the node's constrains list, so mechanical.chassis is owed a follow-up. control.tilt_estimator.json (new node, rev 29) requires the IMU to run 'at an LSM6DS33 output data rate above four times the 100 Hz loop rate' (416 Hz), yet firmware.imu_driver.json -- named directly in control.tilt_estimator's own constrains list -- was rewritten in the same change set (journal.jsonl rev 30) with sample_rate left at 208 Hz and its stale 'normal-mode... above twice the balance-task rate' source untouched, with no no_change_justified entry. 208 Hz does not meet the >400 Hz premise the new node's own source states. By contrast, control.balance_loop and electrical.regulator_5v, also constrained by changed upstream nodes in this same revision, each received specific no_change_justified reasons. The revision is therefore internally inconsistent: it wrote a requirement on firmware.imu_driver that firmware.imu_driver's own (also-rewritten) record does not satisfy and does not explain away.

control.tilt_estimator (new node) constrains both control.balance_loop and firmware.imu_driver. The control.balance_loop edge is followed up with a specific no_change_justified reason, and the electrical.imu -> electrical.control_board / electrical.regulator_5v edges are followed up with value changes or specific reasons. But the control.tilt_estimator -> firmware.imu_driver edge has neither: firmware.imu_driver was rewritten (journal rev 30) with its value and source left byte-identical to rev 26, with no no_change_justified entry addressing why the new 416 Hz estimator requirement has no effect on the 208 Hz driver rate it is supposed to constrain.

control.tilt_estimator's source states the complementary filter is 'updated on every gyro sample, at an LSM6DS33 output data rate above four times the 100 Hz loop rate' (i.e. above 400 Hz, using 416 Hz). firmware.imu_driver's own recorded value, rewritten in this same change set, is 208 Hz with source 'highest LSM6DS33 normal-mode output data rate, above twice the balance-task rate' -- 208 Hz is below the 400 Hz premise the new node's source states, directly contradicting it.

The revision is internally inconsistent: control.balance_loop's new speed_limit quantity now constrains both mechanical.gearbox_left and mechanical.gearbox_right (design/nodes/control.balance_loop.json, diff hunk 2, constrains list), but only gearbox_right received a follow-up quantity (input_speed_limit, design/nodes/mechanical.gearbox_right.json diff hunk 6). mechanical.gearbox_left.json's rev-31 payload (diff hunk 5) is byte-identical to its pre-revision rev-5 payload — no new quantity, no no_change_justified entry naming control.balance_loop. control.balance_loop added a new quantity (speed_limit) and a new constrains edge to both mechanical.gearbox_left and mechanical.gearbox_right (design/nodes/control.balance_loop.json diff). mechanical.gearbox_right received a follow-up quantity (input_speed_limit = 51.3 rad/s). mechanical.gearbox_left's rev-31 payload is byte-identical to its pre-revision rev-5 payload (diff hunk for mechanical.gearbox_left.json shows no field changed) and carries no no_change_justified entry for control.balance_loop. The edge to mechanical.gearbox_left therefore has neither a follow-up change nor a stated reason, which is a finding 'as usual' per the rubric preamble ([rule]–[rule] are not excused by the Unwritten-records rule).

design/nodes/electrical.imu.json: the newly written 'standby_current_draw' (value 6, unit mA, source the LSM6DS33 datasheet) is inconsistent with its own cited source -- parts_sheet.json row R8.08 ('power-down current') gives 6 uA for that same datasheet, not 6 mA -- and is inconsistent with the sibling 'current_draw' value of 0.9 mA (active mode) in the same node, since a standby current cannot physically exceed the active current. The revision's own written value fails to hold together with its source and with its own other written data.

design/nodes/electrical.imu.json's new standby_current_draw record is {value: 6, unit: "mA", source: https://www.pololu.com/file/0J1087/LSM6DS33.pdf}. parts_sheet.json row R8.08 ('power-down current'), from the same datasheet URL, gives {value: 6, unit: "uA"}. The revision copied the number but changed the unit without converting -- a 1000x magnitude error -- and the resulting figure (6 mA standby) exceeds the node's own 0.9 mA active current_draw, which is physically impossible for a power-down state. This is the conversion arithmetic itself failing, a derived-bound (category 1) violation.

mechanical.chassis.json's mass changed from 165g (prior revision, journal.jsonl rev 4) to 205g (this revision, rev 29) via the new source 'derived: [R11.01]-[R10.03]+[R9.03]*[R9.06]'. R11.01-R10.03 (200g-35g=165g) already includes the wheel-pair mass -- per the skill file's own citation of Pololu product 3575 as '200 g assembled with motors, 80 mm wheels and bumper cage', and confirmed by mechanical.frame_and_board.json's formula which subtracts [R9.03]*[R9.06] from that same baseline to isolate the bare frame+board (106g = 200-35-39.7-19). Adding [R9.03]*[R9.06] again on top of the 165g baseline double-counts the ~39.7g wheel-pair mass, giving the erroneous 205g. mechanical.assembly.json's accompanying no_change_justified entry ('A dimension was added to the chassis; no part was added or moved, so the unladen and total masses are unchanged') is contradicted by this very 40g mass change written in the same revision. The revision is therefore inconsistent with the design graph it modifies.

mechanical.chassis.json's new mass (205g) does not reconcile with its sourced neighbors: mechanical.wheel_pair.json (mass 39.7g, constrains mechanical.chassis) and mechanical.frame_and_board.json (mass 106g, constrains mechanical.chassis) already sum with two motors (R1.21*R1.25=19g) to 164.7g ~= the chassis's prior 165g value. The new formula adds [R9.03]*[R9.06] (~39.7g) a second time on top of that already-complete 165g baseline, double-counting the wheel-pair's mass by about 40g. This is a magnitude inconsistent with the values it depends on.

mechanical.chassis's mass changed from 165g to 205g, and mechanical.chassis.json's 'constrains' lists 'mechanical.assembly'. mechanical.assembly.json does carry a non-empty no_change_justified entry for mechanical.chassis, but the reason given ('no part was added or moved, so the unladen and total masses are unchanged') is contradicted by the numbers: mechanical.chassis's own mass value changed by 40g in this same revision. A reason contradicted by the numbers is a finding per cross §5 / std application.

mechanical.chassis.json's mass (written this revision) is meant to come from a stated parts list/method, but the method no longer reconciles with that list: mechanical.wheel_pair.json (39.7g) and mechanical.frame_and_board.json (106g) plus two motors (19g) already sum to the chassis's prior total (164.7g ~= 165g, via R11.01-R10.03). The new formula double-counts the wheel-pair term, so the mass written for this module is no longer consistent with the parts list that underlies it.

design/nodes/mechanical.gearbox_left.json's new `motor_reaction_moment` (0.145 N*m, derived: [R1.07]*[R1.25]) and design/nodes/mechanical.gearbox_right.json's new `motor_reaction_moment` (0.0726 N*m, Pololu product-3073 datasheet) are both new values this revision wrote (journal.jsonl revs 29-30) for structurally symmetric siblings, yet differ by a factor of 2 with no stated reason; their sum (0.2176 N*m) does not equal mechanical.chassis.json's declared total `reaction_moment` of 0.145 N*m, and chassis's own new `no_change_justified` text (journal rev 31) -- written by this same revision -- asserts each side's share is 0.0726 N*m, directly contradicting the 0.145 N*m it actually wrote for gearbox_left. The revision is therefore inconsistent with the design it changes.

design/nodes/mechanical.gearbox_left.json and design/nodes/mechanical.gearbox_right.json both carry `motor_reaction_moment` for the two mirror-image halves of the same drivetrain (same gear_ratio 2.88, same overall_gear_ratio 148.3, same motor model), yet the values are 0.145 N*m and 0.0726 N*m respectively -- a 2x discrepancy with no stated design reason. [rule] requires judging a magnitude against its neighbours (explicitly including 'a reaction against the load'); these two neighbouring, nominally identical components fail that comparison.

mechanical.chassis.json declares a total `reaction_moment` of 0.145 N*m, and its own `no_change_justified` text (journal.jsonl rev 31) states this total is the sum of the two gearboxes' per-side reactions. Summing the two gearboxes' actually-declared reactions, mechanical.gearbox_left.json's 0.145 N*m and mechanical.gearbox_right.json's 0.0726 N*m, gives 0.2176 N*m, not 0.145 N*m: the declared reactions do not balance the declared total by about 0.073 N*m (roughly 50% of the stated total). This is a derived-bound (equilibrium) failure, never relaxable.

mechanical.gearbox_left and mechanical.gearbox_right both changed (gained `motor_reaction_moment`) and both `constrains` mechanical.chassis, control.balance_loop and firmware.encoder_counter (design/nodes/mechanical.gearbox_left.json, mechanical.gearbox_right.json). Follow-up `no_change_justified` reasons were written to all three constrained nodes (journal.jsonl revs 31-33). The reason on mechanical.chassis.json -- 'the two per-side reactions of 0.0726 N*m sum to the chassis total of 0.145 N*m already carried' -- is contradicted by the numbers actually written (gearbox_left's own reaction is 0.145 N*m, not 0.0726 N*m, see [rule]/[rule]), which is explicitly named in the rubric as a finding ('a reason that is empty, generic, or contradicted by the numbers is a finding').

The newly written `motor_reaction_moment` on both mechanical.gearbox_left.json and mechanical.gearbox_right.json is sourced from the gearmotor's 6V-rated stall torque (parts_sheet.json R1.07 'stall torque @ 6V', and the product-3073/specs datasheet, also a 6V rating), with no stated basis for applying a 6V figure to this design, which the design graph itself records as running at 7.2V nominal (parts_sheet.json R5.03, used for electrical.battery_pack.supply_voltage in journal rev 10). [rule] and the skill file's load-case procedure (step 2) require the stall-torque reaction to be taken 'at the voltage the design runs at'; the skill file's own worked example flags this exact gap ('the kit runs at 7.2 V nominal on NiMH, not the rating's 6 V, so that bound needs a stated basis there'). Neither written value states that basis.

design/nodes/mechanical.gearbox_left.json and mechanical.gearbox_right.json each got their own independently-sourced `motor_reaction_moment` (0.145 N*m via a derived formula; 0.0726 N*m via a datasheet URL), and design/nodes/mechanical.chassis.json got its own `no_change_justified` claim that the two sum to its total -- but nowhere in the design graph is there a calculation that actually takes gearbox_left, gearbox_right and chassis together and checks the sum; the chassis's own claimed sum (0.0726+0.0726=0.145) does not match what was actually written for gearbox_left (0.145, not 0.0726), and the mismatch (shown under [rule]) was never caught because no assembly-level check was performed. This is feature isolation at the gearbox-to-chassis mounting interface, confirmed directly from the design graph with no missing interface input (the chassis total and both gearbox values are all present and readable).

The revision's own two writes are internally inconsistent: mechanical.assembly.mass (365 g, rev 29) no longer equals mechanical.assembly.unladen_mass (165 g, unchanged) plus the battery mass (165 g) as it did before the revision (330 g); and the no_change_justified reason the revision attached to control.balance_loop ('the plant mass is unchanged') is directly contradicted by that very same mass having changed by 35 g (10.6%) in mechanical.assembly in the same changeset. Both defects are in what the revision itself wrote, so per clause B this is [rule]'s job to catch, and it is unmet.

mechanical.assembly.mass (365 g) is inconsistent with its own node's neighbour quantity unladen_mass (165 g) plus the battery mass (165 g) = 330 g, a 35 g (10.6%) gap with no stated reason; it is also inconsistent with control.balance_loop.plant_mass (330 g), the sibling node's own copy of the same physical quantity, written in the same changeset (design/journal.jsonl lines 29-30). No explanation anywhere accounts for the 35 g difference, which is exactly R10.03 (bumper-cage mass, 35 g), the term the new formula silently stopped subtracting.

mechanical.assembly.mass changed from 330 g to 365 g (a physically different number, not a re-save), and mechanical.assembly constrains control.balance_loop. The revision supplies a no_change_justified entry on control.balance_loop keyed 'mechanical.assembly': 'Only overall dimensions were added; the plant mass is unchanged, and the sheet gives no centre-of-mass height for the loop to use.' That reason is contradicted by the numbers: the plant mass is not unchanged, mass rose by 35 g (10.6%) in the very same write. Per [rule]'s own text, 'a reason...contradicted by the numbers is a finding.'

The revision writes mass, a mass property std §11 names explicitly as a cross quantity 'owned by sizing' (ARCH-051): 'mass, centre-of-mass height above the axle and pitch inertia...are cross quantities owned by sizing.' mechanical.assembly.json's rewritten mass quantity carries written_by: 'mechanical' (design/journal.jsonl line 29), i.e. a mechanical-domain write of a quantity std §11 marks cross-owned, matching [rule]'s explicit sub-check: 'A mechanical session writing a quantity marked cross itself is a finding.' Because mass's value and source changed, the whole quantity record (including written_by) is a written value under the Verdict policy's 'Given and written values' rule, so this sub-check is judged normally rather than as a given-value or unwritten-record case.

The no_change_justified text the revision wrote on control.balance_loop states 'the plant mass is unchanged,' a claim about the design state; the design graph itself (the same changeset, design/journal.jsonl lines 29-30) shows mechanical.assembly.mass rose from 330 g to 365 g, directly contradicting that claim. Per [rule]'s 'Confirmed when' clause, a claim that contradicts the observation it cites, where the value/text is one the work wrote, is confirmed; the contradiction is visible in the design graph alone, satisfying clause B's requirement that the revision or design graph (not only a trajectory) show it.

The no_change_justified reason on control.balance_loop ('Only overall dimensions were added; the plant mass is unchanged...') is exactly the pattern [rule] names: 'a no_change_justified reason written to avoid a follow-up rather than because none is owed.' The design graph itself shows both the choice (the stated reason) and that it is false (mechanical.assembly.mass changed by 35 g in the same changeset), which under clause B is sufficient to confirm this indicator without needing a trajectory, since the revision avoided the follow-up [rule] would otherwise require.

The revision is not consistent with the design it changes or with this rubric: electrical.mcu's new max_supply_voltage (60 V, design/nodes/electrical.mcu.json, journal.jsonl line 29) does not match the 6.0 V its own cited Microchip datasheet source gives via parts_sheet.json row R7.09 ('MCU maximum operating voltage (abs. max)', value 6.0, unit V, same datasheet URL) -- a magnitude error ([rule]). Separately, the new supply_voltage_margin quantity uses that same Absolute-Maximum-Ratings-table figure (R7.09) as the operating limit against the board's 5 V logic supply (R7.03), which is precisely the 'absolute maximum rating used as an operating limit' antipattern the electrical standards rule 1 and skill file forbid ([rule], [rule]). These are rejecting findings against the revision's own written values, not against any given value.

Trigger: the revision adds a new rating, max_supply_voltage, to electrical.mcu (journal.jsonl line 29). Its record gives only {value: 60, unit: V, source: Microchip ATmega16U4/32U4 datasheet URL, written_by: electrical} with no stated condition (temperature, supply voltage, duty cycle, board or mounting) under which that rating was taken, as [rule] (§1) requires for a newly added rating. This is the work's own duty (the rubric's verdict policy names [rule] explicitly as a duty of the work, not a missing input), so its absence is a finding.

Trigger: a rating (electrical.mcu.max_supply_voltage / the R7.09 figure it is built from) is compared with an operating value (electrical.mcu.supply_voltage = 5 V) via the new supply_voltage_margin quantity (journal.jsonl line 29, source 'derived: [R7.09] - [R7.03]'). parts_sheet.json's R7.09 row is explicitly labelled 'MCU maximum operating voltage (abs. max)', i.e. an Absolute Maximum Ratings-table figure, used here as the limit. Per §1 and [rule], the limit must be the recommended operating condition, not the absolute maximum; this fails.

electrical.mcu.max_supply_voltage is recorded as 60 V, sourced to the Microchip ATmega16U4/32U4 datasheet (journal.jsonl line 29). parts_sheet.json's R7.09 row, citing the identical datasheet URL for 'MCU maximum operating voltage (abs. max)', gives 6.0 V. The written value (60 V) is not the number its cited source gives -- a factor-of-10 magnitude error -- which fails [rule] (cross §1, §3; cat. 2, and cat. 1 for the wrong-conversion/prefix-type error).

electrical.mcu.supply_voltage_margin (journal.jsonl line 29) is computed as [R7.09] - [R7.03], where R7.09 is parts_sheet.json's 'MCU maximum operating voltage (abs. max)' row (an Absolute Maximum Ratings-table figure) and R7.03 is the board's actual 5 V logic supply. Using the abs.-max figure as the comparison limit against an operating value is exactly the antipattern 'designing to the absolute maximum rating' (skill file, §1); counts.

The revision's one substantive written value, electrical.battery_pack.motor_runtime (design/nodes/electrical.battery_pack.json, journal.jsonl rev 29), has unit arithmetic that does not balance: [R5.03]*[R5.06]/([R1.01]*[R1.19]*[R4.19]) = 7.2 V * 2.2 A*h / (6 V * 0.42 A * 2) = 15.84 W*h / 5.04 W = 3.14 hours, but the node records unit 's' with value 3.14 — a 3600x discrepancy. This is inconsistent with the design's own cited arithmetic and with cross-domain standards §2 ('unit arithmetic is exact') and electrical standards [rule]/[rule] (cat. 1, never relaxed), so the revision is not consistent with the design it changes or with this rubric.

electrical.battery_pack.json, motor_runtime quantity (journal.jsonl rev 29): source 'derived: [R5.03] * [R5.06] / ([R1.01] * [R1.19] * [R4.19])' with [R5.03]=7.2 V, [R5.06]=2.2 A*h, [R1.01]=6 V, [R1.19]=0.42 A, [R4.19]=2 gives (V*A*h)/(V*A) = h, i.e. 15.84 W*h / 5.04 W = 3.14 hours. The record states unit 's' with value 3.14 — the unit arithmetic does not balance; the stated unit is wrong by a factor of 3600 relative to the cited formula's own dimensions.

The same motor_runtime record: redone with correct unit tracking the formula gives ≈3.14 h ≈ 11,314 s, not 3.14 s. The recorded magnitude (3.14, unit s) is not what its cited source/derivation gives once units are carried through — a wrong conversion (cross §2; cat. 1).

electrical.driver_left.json 'no_load_current_draw' = 125, unit 'A', source 'derived: [R1.02] * [R1.06] / [R5.03]' (6 V * 150 mA / 7.2 V = 125 mA = 0.125 A, not 125 A); electrical.driver_right.json records the same formula correctly as 0.125 A. The two structurally identical nodes disagree by a factor of 1000 on the same derivation, and driver_left's value (125 A) exceeds its own current_limit (1.8 A) and the motor's stall current (1.5 A, parts_sheet.json R1.04) by roughly two orders of magnitude, which is physically impossible for a no-load current. electrical.battery_pack.json's added no_change_justified text ('the no-load figure lies inside [the stall budget]') is therefore false for driver_left as written. The revision is not consistent with the design it changes (its own sibling node and its own justification text).

electrical.driver_left.json places 'no_load_current_draw' = 125 (unit A) directly beside 'current_limit' = 1.8 A on the same node. Redoing the comparison by reading: 125 A is far above the 1.8 A rating it sits beside, so the budget does not close for this newly written quantity; the figure is also inconsistent with the sibling node's correctly computed 0.125 A for the identical formula and part.

electrical.driver_left.json 'no_load_current_draw': source 'derived: [R1.02] * [R1.06] / [R5.03]' = 6 V * 150 mA / 7.2 V, which by unit arithmetic (V * mA / V = mA) gives 125 mA, i.e. 0.125 A; the record instead gives value 125 with unit 'A', a mismatch between the stated unit and the arithmetic's actual resultant unit (a dropped mA-to-A conversion).

electrical.driver_left.json 'no_load_current_draw' = 125 A does not match what its cited source computes: 6 V * 150 mA / 7.2 V = 0.125 A, not 125 A -- off by a factor of 1000 (a unit-prefix/conversion error), exactly the magnitude-vs-source defect this item targets.

Redoing the balance by reading: electrical.driver_left.json declares no_load_current_draw = 125 A on the same node as current_limit = 1.8 A; 125 A vastly exceeds every current figure on this node and in the design (stall current 1.5 A, pack motor_current_draw 2.5 A total), so the declared draw does not balance against any declared supply/limit figure it sits beside.

electrical.driver_left.json 'no_load_current_draw' = 125, unit 'A', while its own cited source formula computes 6 V * 150 mA / 7.2 V = 0.125 A; this written value decides the battery_pack.no_change_justified conclusion that 'the no-load figure lies inside [the stall budget]', a conclusion the written 125 A value actually fails (125 A > 1.25 A stall budget) even though its cited source gives a different, passing value (0.125 A).

electrical.battery_pack.json's no_change_justified text claims the driver_left no-load figure 'lies inside' the 1.25 A stall budget; this claim contradicts the design's own written value, electrical.driver_left.no_load_current_draw = 125 A, which is far outside (above) that budget, not inside it.

electrical.battery_cell.energy_capacity is written as value 2.64, unit 'J', from 'derived: [R5.05]*[R5.06]' (1.2 V x 2.2 A*h = 2.64 W*h, not J); electrical.battery_pack's own no_change_justified text (journal rev 30) then calls this same quantity '2.64 W*h', contradicting the unit the revision itself wrote. electrical.battery_cell.energy_capacity (design/nodes/electrical.battery_cell.json; journal rev 29) is recorded as value 2.64, unit 'J', source 'derived: [R5.05] * [R5.06]' where R5.05 = 1.2 V and R5.06 = 2200 mA*h (2.2 A*h). design/nodes/electrical.imu.json's written current_draw record is {"source":"https://www.pololu.com/file/0J1087/LSM6DS33.pdf","unit":"mW","value":1.25}. parts_sheet.json row R8.04 (the same datasheet, same number) is explicitly "supply current, gyro + accel high-performance mode", value 1.25, unit "mA" — a current, not a power. design/nodes/electrical.control_board.json's own derivation, "derived: [R8.03] * [R8.04]" = 3.3 V * 1.25 = 4.13 mW, treats R8.04 as a current multiplied by voltage to yield power, confirming R8.04 (and hence electrical.imu.current_draw) is a current in mA, not a power in mW. The unit on the written electrical.imu.current_draw record is wrong: a current-named quantity carries a power unit. This is a confirmed, evidenced unit-record error, judged by reading as the rubric requires.

design/nodes/firmware.balance_task.json: the 'sample_rate' field was changed from {"unit":"Hz","value":100} (journal rev 25) to {"unit":"ms","value":2.5} (journal rev 30), while every other 'sample_rate' quantity in the graph (control.balance_loop rev 29: 400 Hz; firmware.imu_driver rev 31: 833 Hz; control.req_loop_rate rev 20: 100 Hz) stays in Hz. control.balance_loop's newly written 'torque_limit' (journal.jsonl rev29, design/nodes/control.balance_loop.json) is sourced 'derived: [R1.18] * [R1.25]' = 0.16 kgf*cm * 2 = 0.32 (in kgf*cm), but is recorded with value 0.32 and unit 'N*m' with no kgf*cm->N*m conversion applied. The sibling quantity in the same node, 'torque_peak' (source 'derived: [R1.07] * [R1.25]' = 0.74 kgf*cm * 2 = 1.48 kgf*cm), correctly converts to 0.145 N*m (1.48 * 0.0980665 = 0.1451). Applying the identical, design-established conversion to torque_limit gives 0.16*2*0.0980665 = 0.0314 N*m, not 0.32 N*m -- an order-of-magnitude (~10.2x) unit-arithmetic error. The result is also physically inconsistent with the design's own figures: the written 'limit' (0.32 N*m) exceeds the motor's own stall-torque-derived 'torque_peak' (0.145 N*m), which no actuator can produce. This contradicts cross-domain standard section 2 ('unit arithmetic is exact') and the design's own precedent in the same node, so the revision is not consistent with the design it changes.

control.balance_loop's torque_limit (journal.jsonl rev29) carries a unit ('N*m') and a source string ('derived: [R1.18] * [R1.25]'), but the recorded value (0.32) does not match that source's own arithmetic once the parts sheet's kilogram_force*cm unit is correctly converted to N*m: R1.18 (0.16 kgf*cm, parts_sheet.json) * R1.25 (2) * 0.0980665 (kgf*cm->N*m) = 0.0314 N*m, not 0.32. The sibling torque_peak quantity in the same node performs this exact conversion correctly (0.74*2*0.0980665 = 0.145 N*m), confirming the convention torque_limit failed to follow. The quantity's source therefore does not actually support its recorded value.

Claimed: control.balance_loop torque_limit = 0.32 N*m, source 'derived: [R1.18] * [R1.25]' (journal.jsonl rev29). Observation that contradicts it: R1.18 = 0.16 kilogram_force*cm and R1.25 = 2 (parts_sheet.json); correctly converting kgf*cm to N*m with the same factor the design's own sibling quantity torque_peak uses (0.0980665, verified by 0.74*2*0.0980665 = 0.145 matching the recorded torque_peak) gives 0.16*2*0.0980665 = 0.0314 N*m, not 0.32 N*m. The stated source does not support the recorded value.

The new speed_limit quantity carries a unit, rad per s, and a source field, the pololu product 3073 specs URL, but the source does not support the value. The node writes speed_limit at 513 rad per s sourced to the pololu product 3073 specs page, the identical URL already cited for no_load_speed at 68.1 rad per s in the same node. electrical.motor_left.json (journal rev 29) records efficiency_point_output_power as {"source":"https://www.pololu.com/product/3073/specs","unit":"J","value":0.8}; electrical.motor_right.json (journal rev 30), written in the same revision from the same source and with the same value 0.8, records the identical quantity as {"unit":"W",...}. firmware.imu_driver.json (journal.jsonl rev 31) sets quantities.sample_rate = 8330 Hz, sourced 'design: lowest LSM6DS33 output data rate above twice the 300 Hz balance-task rate; requires high-performance mode.' The LSM6DS33's output-data-rate steps double from 12.5 Hz to a maximum of about 6.66 kHz (12.5/26/52/104/208/416/833/1660/3330/6660 Hz); the same node's own prior, unmodified value of 208 Hz (visible in journal.jsonl rev 26) is itself one of these steps, confirming the progression. The lowest step above twice 300 Hz (600 Hz) is 833 Hz, not 8330 Hz, and 8330 Hz also exceeds the sensor's actual maximum rate, so it describes a configuration the named part cannot physically achieve. The written value contradicts both its own stated rationale and the physical limits of the cited sensor, so the revision is not consistent with the design it changes.

Redoing the bound I_stall,max = V_max/R with R = V_rated/I_stall = 6 V/1.5 A = 4 Ω (from electrical.motor_left/motor_right, unchanged) and V_max = 9 V (electrical.battery_pack.supply_voltage, written by this revision), the true stall current is 9/4 = 2.25 A per motor. The revision's written electrical.driver_left/driver_right.current_draw instead fell to 1.0 A (from 1.25 A at the prior 7.2 V pack) via the formula [R1.02]*[R1.04]/[R5.04] = power-at-rated-voltage divided by pack voltage -- a figure that decreases as supply voltage increases, the opposite of the correct scaling, and well below the correctly-scaled 2.25 A.

No comparison of the corrected stall current (2.25 A per motor, see [rule]) against electrical.driver_left/driver_right.current_limit (1.8 A, given) or the DRV8838's minimum OCP trip (~1.9 A, per the skill file) is shown anywhere in the revision; the written current_draw (1.0 A) is below both ratings and so the required 'driver's behaviour stated and declared to control/firmware' step never triggers, even though the correctly-scaled current exceeds both.

Before this revision, electrical.battery_pack declared charge_capacity (2.2 A*h) and energy_capacity (15.8 W*h) as the supply's rating (design/nodes/electrical.battery_pack.json, journal rev 10). The revision's rewritten battery_pack (rev 30) and battery_cell (rev 29) omit these fields entirely and source no replacement for the new (alkaline-voltage) chemistry, so the supply's rating is no longer declared and the balance against draw cannot be redone, as [rule] requires.

The budget's only current/power entries (electrical.battery_pack.motor_current_draw = 2.0 A, electrical.driver_left/right.current_draw = 1.0 A) are derived from rated-voltage stall power divided by the new pack voltage, which behaves like an average/continuous figure, not the true coincident worst-case stall current at the pack's highest voltage (2.25 A per motor, per [rule]); the true worst case is absent from the written budget without a stated reason.

electrical.battery_pack.supply_voltage (9 V nominal) is the only voltage used to compute electrical.driver_left/driver_right.current_draw and electrical.battery_cell.rated_voltage; no check is made at the top (highest open-circuit voltage) or the sagged bottom of the alkaline pack's voltage window.

The written driver current_draw at the new, higher pack voltage (1.0 A at 9 V) is lower than the motor's rated-voltage stall current (1.5 A at 6 V) even though the pack runs at 1.5x the motor's rated voltage; stall current was not scaled up with the pack's higher voltage as the driver-vs-motor check requires.

The data needed to check a motor stall against the driver's limits sits in separate nodes that are never cross-checked in the final state: electrical.motor_left/motor_right give stall_current = 1.5 A at rated_voltage = 6 V (giving R = 4 Ω); electrical.battery_pack.supply_voltage (written) is now 9 V; electrical.driver_left/driver_right.current_limit = 1.8 A (given). Reading these together by the skill file's own method gives a true stall current of 2.25 A per motor, which exceeds the driver's 1.8 A peak rating and its ~1.9 A OCP trip -- a stall that would trip the driver -- yet this is never checked across the nodes in the final state, and nothing in firmware.motor_output or any control node declares this trip condition to the control/firmware roles, matching the [rule] observable 'a stall that trips the driver not declared to the control or firmware role.' The failing combination uses battery_pack.supply_voltage, a value the revision wrote.

firmware.imu_driver.json raises sample_rate from 208 Hz to 416 Hz and states this 'requires high-performance mode', but no node anywhere in design/nodes/ (in particular electrical.imu.json, which carries only current_draw and supply_voltage) states or sources an anti-aliasing/low-pass filter bandwidth for the IMU, either before or after the change. [rule](a) requires the configured filter bandwidth to sit below half the rate the firmware uses the samples at, sourced against the datasheet; because the revision itself chose the new, higher rate, this gap is the revision's own (see [rule] below), making the revision inconsistent with this rubric's [rule](a) requirement even though its arithmetic, sourcing and cross-domain follow-up ([rule], [rule]) are otherwise sound.

firmware.imu_driver.json's sample_rate rose from 208 Hz to 416 Hz (journal rev 29, 'requires high-performance mode'), and electrical.imu.json's current_draw was correctly updated to 1.25 mA matching parts_sheet.json row R8.04 ('supply current, gyro + accel high-performance mode'). Sub-check (a) requires the configured anti-aliasing/low-pass filter bandwidth to sit below half the rate the firmware uses the samples at, sourced against the datasheet; no node in design/nodes/ states or sources any filter-bandwidth quantity for the IMU at either rate, and since the revision itself chose the new rate (a written value), this absence is the revision's own duty, not a missing design input, so (a) is unmet. Sub-check (b) is satisfied by reading: control.balance_loop.json's 100 Hz loop is well below the IMU's 416 Hz rate, so the loop cannot be treating a repeated read as a new sample. Sub-checks (c1) and (c2) need the plant's unstable pole p, which the account states the parts sheet gives for no part (a stand-in absence), so they are recorded non-blocking (see spec_defects) rather than unmet. Sub-check (c3) needs a measured loop delay, likewise listed as a stand-in absence and recorded non-blocking. The item is unmet overall on sub-check (a).

design/nodes/firmware.balance_task.json lists control.balance_loop in its constrains array and its sample_rate was changed (100->400 Hz, journal rev30); design/nodes/electrical.imu.json also lists control.balance_loop in its constrains array and its current_draw was changed (0.9->1.25 mA, journal rev32). design/nodes/control.balance_loop.json's only write in this revision is rev29, earlier than both, and carries no no_change_justified entry for either edge. firmware.balance_task.json (constrains firmware.imu_driver and control.balance_loop, sample_rate changed at journal rev30) and electrical.imu.json (constrains electrical.control_board and control.balance_loop, current_draw changed at journal rev32) both name control.balance_loop as a constrained node, but control.balance_loop.json's only write in this revision is the earlier rev29, and it carries no no_change_justified entry naming either firmware.balance_task or electrical.imu. electrical.imu.json's current_draw changed from 0.9 mA to 1.25 mA (diff hunk, electrical.imu.json; journal.jsonl rev 17 -> rev 33) and its constrains list names both electrical.control_board and control.balance_loop. control.req_loop_rate.json's sample_rate source reads 'design: lowest balance-loop rate the robot is specified to run at, raised for tighter tilt regulation' and control.balance_loop.json's reads 'design: control period of about 6.7 ms, meeting the required minimum loop rate' -- neither cites a closed-loop crossover frequency, natural frequency, or any numeric ratio to the delivered loop's frequency anywhere in the design graph; the justification is a qualitative performance goal, not a stated ratio, matching [rule]'s antipattern directly.

The revision is inconsistent with this rubric: it weakens control.req_loop_rate's sample-rate floor from 100 Hz to 50 Hz (journal rev29; design/nodes/control.req_loop_rate.json) for an open-loop-unstable plant with no sourced stability analysis anywhere in the design graph to show the lower floor is safe, and with no issued specification able to supply an allowance (rule 10: 'with no issued specification there are no allowances'). design/journal.jsonl rev29 and design/nodes/control.req_loop_rate.json: the required minimum balance-loop rate, a 'kind': 'requirement' node whose sole purpose is to constrain control.balance_loop, was lowered from 100 Hz to 50 Hz with the stated reason 'relaxed to admit slower test builds' and no sourced stability analysis anywhere in the design graph showing 50 Hz remains adequate for this open-loop-unstable plant.

design/nodes/firmware.fall_detector.json's sample_rate (13 Hz, source 'design: lowest LSM6DS33 output data rate') is inconsistent with the source it cites: the LSM6DS33's documented ODR options are 12.5, 26, 52, 104, 208, 416, 833 Hz, 1.66 kHz, 3.33 kHz, 6.66 kHz -- there is no 13 Hz setting, and the lowest is 12.5 Hz (which the account's own 'written to three significant figures' rule would render as 12.5, not 13). design/nodes/firmware.fall_detector.json's sample_rate is written as 13 Hz with source 'design: lowest LSM6DS33 output data rate', but the LSM6DS33's documented ODR table (12.5, 26, 52, 104, 208, 416, 833 Hz, 1.66/3.33/6.66 kHz) has no 13 Hz option; the actual lowest rate is 12.5 Hz. The value is a magnitude unsupported by the source it cites, which the verdict policy explicitly treats as a finding regardless of whether a record was otherwise required of the revision.

The revision's supply_voltage_margin quantity on electrical.mcu is built from R7.09, the parts sheet's 'abs. max' row, used as the limit against the operating supply voltage. This is inconsistent with electrical standards §1 (absolute maximum ratings are stress ratings only, not operating limits) and fails [rule], so the revision is not consistent with the design's own standards.

The new max_supply_voltage record on electrical.mcu carries only {value: 6.0, unit: V, source: <Microchip datasheet URL>}; no condition (temperature, duty cycle, board or mounting) is recorded for this rating, as §1 requires.

max_supply_voltage (6.0 V) is copied from parts_sheet row R7.09, titled 'MCU maximum operating voltage (abs. max)' — the datasheet's Absolute Maximum Ratings table entry — and is then used as the limit in supply_voltage_margin = R7.09 − R7.03 = 1.0 V, i.e. compared directly against the 5 V operating supply voltage. Per §1 and [rule], an absolute-maximum figure used this way as an operating limit fails.

The new max_supply_voltage quantity is taken directly from parts_sheet row R7.09, titled 'MCU maximum operating voltage (abs. max)' — the Absolute Maximum Ratings table entry — and that figure is then used as the comparison limit in supply_voltage_margin. This is designing/margining to the absolute maximum rating, the skill file's first antipattern.

The revision is internally well-formed (correct units, correct arithmetic, a specific non-generic follow-up reason discharging [rule]) but is not fully consistent with this rubric: the new, revision-written `no_load_current_draw` quantity, and the `no_change_justified` comparison that relies on it, use only the battery pack's nominal voltage (source row R5.03 = 7.2 V) with no corresponding figure at the top (charged, highest open-circuit) or sagged-bottom voltage of the window, which is exactly the single-battery-voltage antipattern ([rule]) and standards violation ([rule]) described below.

The revision writes no_load_current_draw for both drivers using only the pack's nominal voltage (source row R5.03 = 7.2 V); the battery_pack.no_change_justified text explicitly relies on comparing this nominal-voltage no-load figure against the (also nominal-voltage) stall budget to conclude no propagation is needed. No check of either figure is performed at the top (charged, highest open-circuit voltage) or the sagged bottom of the window, as [rule] requires ('A check at nominal voltage only fails'). Because this comparison is built from a value the revision itself wrote (no_load_current_draw), it is judged normally, not shielded by the given-value rule.

The newly written no_load_current_draw (0.125 A on both driver_left and driver_right) is computed solely from the pack's nominal voltage (parts_sheet row R5.03 = 7.2 V); the battery_pack.no_change_justified comparison that uses it to decide no propagation is needed is likewise evaluated only at that one voltage, with no corresponding figure or check at the top of the window (highest open-circuit/charged voltage, which the skill file's own example puts at about 8.4 V for this six-cell NiMH pack) or at the sagged bottom. This is exactly the 'one battery voltage' antipattern, built from a value the revision wrote, so it is judged normally and counts.

The numeric propagation is internally correct (design/nodes/control.req_loop_rate.json, control.balance_loop.json, firmware.balance_task.json, firmware.imu_driver.json, electrical.imu.json, electrical.control_board.json, electrical.regulator_5v.json all check out arithmetically and via constrains follow-up), so the revision is consistent with the design it changes. Because the revision itself authored this inadequate justification text, this is not an exempt given-value/unwritten-record/stand-in-absence condition, so [rule] is unmet.

control.req_loop_rate.json and control.balance_loop.json carry new source text for the 120 Hz rate ('lowest balance-loop rate the robot is specified to run at, raised to cut sampling delay in the tilt loop'; 'control period of about 8.3 ms, meeting the required minimum loop rate'). mechanical.chassis.reaction_moment (design/nodes/mechanical.chassis.json, journal rev 35) was written as 0.108 N*m, citing 'https://www.pololu.com/product/3074/specs' directly, i.e. the new motor's single-motor stall torque (R1a.13 = 1.1 kgf*cm = 0.108 N*m) with no x2-motors factor. control.balance_loop.torque_peak (design/nodes/control.balance_loop.json, journal rev 37), written in the same revision from the same new motor's stall-torque row, correctly keeps the base design's formula 'derived: [R1a.13] * [R1.25]' = 0.216 N*m. In the base design (journal revs 4 and 21) these two quantities used the identical formula 'derived: [R1.07] * [R1.25]' and were numerically equal at 0.145 N*m each, establishing that they represent the same combined reaction torque. The revision breaks that equality by a factor of 2 for mechanical.chassis alone, with no no_change_justified entry or other stated reason for the divergence. This is an inconsistency within the revision's own written values, not a condition already present in the base (which had the two values equal) nor a given value nor an unwritten record, so the revision is not consistent with the design it changes.

mechanical.chassis's mass (184 g, journal rev 35: derived: [R11.01] - [R10.03] + [R1a.07] * [R1.25]) now exceeds mechanical.assembly's unladen_mass (165 g, journal rev 36: derived: [R11.01] - [R10.03], unchanged) even though the chassis 'constrains' and is part of that unladen assembly, because the revision added a motor-mass term to the chassis formula without reconciling the sibling mechanical.assembly and control.balance_loop (plant_mass, 330 g, also unchanged) formulas that represent the same physical system and were also rewritten in this change set. The written no_change_justified text for mechanical.assembly ('the 30:1 gearmotor weighs the same 9.5 g as the 50:1, so the unladen and total masses are unchanged') misstates why the numbers are unchanged (its own formula never referenced motor mass at all) and does not address the new conflict with chassis.mass. In the base design chassis.mass (165 g) exactly equalled assembly.unladen_mass (165 g); the conflict is new. The revision is therefore not consistent with the design it changes.

mechanical.chassis's mass (184 g, journal rev 35) now exceeds mechanical.assembly's own unladen_mass (165 g, journal rev 36, unchanged), even though mechanical.chassis 'constrains' mechanical.assembly and is a component of that unladen assembly -- a part cannot be more massive than the unladen whole it belongs to. The 19 g excess is exactly the motor-mass term ([R1a.07] x [R1.25] = 9.5 g x 2 = 19 g) the revision added to the chassis formula but not to the assembly's or to control.balance_loop's plant_mass formula. This magnitude does not agree with the design's own other declared values, and is a finding even though both nodes were written by the revision, since a magnitude out of physical sense is judged as a finding regardless of the given-value/unwritten-record shields.

mechanical.gearbox_left and mechanical.gearbox_right both list firmware.encoder_counter in `constrains` and both changed overall_gear_ratio from 148.3 to 127.3 (journal rev29/30). firmware.encoder_counter was rewritten (rev34) but neither received an updated overall_gear_ratio nor gained a no_change_justified entry addressing mechanical.gearbox_left/right. control.speed_controller's no_change_justified entry for 'firmware.encoder_counter' (journal rev35) states 'the new ratio is absorbed in the counter, so the gain is unchanged.' firmware.encoder_counter's own overall_gear_ratio was left at 148.3 (rev34), not updated to 127.3, so the stated reason is false on the data in the same design graph. mechanical.chassis.json's mass was changed from a derived 165 g ('derived: [R11.01]-[R10.03]') to a bare 200 g (R11.01 alone). mechanical.chassis's mass quantity changed from 165 g to 200 g -- a physically different number, not a re-saved identical one -- and mechanical.chassis 'constrains': ['mechanical.assembly'] (design/nodes/mechanical.chassis.json). mechanical.assembly was not written in this revision (absent from diff-01-of-02.patch and from the new journal.jsonl entries, rev 29-35) and carries no no_change_justified key for 'mechanical.chassis'; its unladen_mass stays at the stale 165 g. firmware.encoder_counter.json: counts_per_revolution=1778 is inconsistent with its own sibling quantity in the same node, overall_gear_ratio=84.4 (the new, correctly-updated ratio); 1778 corresponds only to the old overall ratio chain (51.45 x 2.88 x 12 = 1778.1), so the magnitude does not match either its cited source or its neighbouring quantity.

mechanical.gearbox_left/right's gear_ratio and overall_gear_ratio changed and both constrain mechanical.chassis, control.balance_loop and firmware.encoder_counter (design/journal.jsonl rev 29-30). mechanical.chassis got a sound no_change_justified reason, and control.balance_loop got a correct follow-up (gear_ratio updated to 1.64). The revision is therefore not consistent with the design it changes.

The revision is not consistent with the design it changes: it replaces the NiMH basis (7.2 V, R5.03) with an alkaline basis (9 V, R5.04) across electrical.battery_cell, electrical.battery_pack and both drivers with no stated rationale anywhere in the written nodes or journal, drops the only named cell/part reference (the Pololu product/1003/specs NiMH cell) without naming a replacement part or chemistry, checks the new battery only at its single nominal voltage (no top/bottom window), and leaves firmware.motor_output's pwm_duty_limit (0.833, still keyed to the old 7.2 V figure via [R5.03]) un-reconciled with the new 9 V supply_voltage it is constrained by, implying the motor can now see 7.5 V average against its 6 V rating. electrical.battery_cell.json previously cited a specific, named part (https://www.pololu.com/product/1003/specs, a Pololu NiMH AA cell, with rated_voltage, charge_capacity and mass_per_cell all drawn from that product page). Every check on the new battery basis (driver current_draw = [R1.02]*[R1.04]/[R5.04], battery_pack.supply_voltage = 9 V) uses the single nominal value (9 V) only; no part is checked at the top (highest open-circuit voltage) or the sagged bottom, and 'a check at nominal voltage only fails' per §4/[rule] independent of the sag-arithmetic sub-check (which is separately blocked by missing internal-resistance data, see spec defects). Because supply_voltage's written number (9 V) differs from the base's (7.2 V), this is judged as a current, non-shielded finding, not a pre-existing condition restated.

electrical.battery_pack constrains firmware.motor_output (per its 'constrains' list). battery_pack.supply_voltage changed from 7.2 V to 9 V in this revision. firmware.motor_output.json was rewritten in the same change set (journal.jsonl rev 33, version 2) but its payload is byte-identical to the prior revision (rev 27): pwm_duty_limit is still 0.833 from 'derived: [R1.02]/[R5.03]' (R5.03 = 7.2 V, the old NiMH nominal), not recomputed against the new 9 V supply, and no no_change_justified entry was added for this edge, nor is any owed follow-up named. Every check against the battery in this revision (driver current_draw formula, battery_pack.supply_voltage) uses the single new nominal voltage (9 V) only; no top (fresh open-circuit) or sagged-bottom value is ever used. electrical.battery_pack.supply_voltage (written, 9 V) and firmware.motor_output.pwm_duty_limit (unchanged, 0.833, still keyed to the old 7.2 V via [R5.03]) each read as internally consistent with their own cited source in isolation, but the combination pwm_duty_limit × supply_voltage = 0.833 × 9 = 7.5 V, checked against the motor's 6 V rated voltage (R1.02), was never checked together anywhere in the design graph and fails when summed by reading; the failing comparison uses battery_pack.supply_voltage, a value the revision wrote.

design/nodes/electrical.imu.json (rev 30) still records current_draw = 0.9 mA (the LSM6DS33 normal-mode figure, R8.05) even though firmware.imu_driver.json (rev 29) raises sample_rate to 416 Hz with the stated reason 'requires high-performance mode', and electrical.control_board.json (rev 31) re-derives sensor_power_draw as [R8.03]*[R8.04] = 4.13 mW, i.e. using the 1.25 mA high-performance-mode current (R8.04) for the very same IMU. control.balance_loop.json's own no_change_justified text ('Only the IMU's supply current changed') confirms the author intended the current to rise, but electrical.imu.current_draw was never updated to 1.25 mA. design/nodes/electrical.imu.json (worktree), current_draw record: unit 'mW', value 1.25, source citing the LSM6DS33 datasheet, written_by electrical. design/nodes/electrical.imu.json (worktree), quantities.current_draw: unit 'mW', value 1.25, source citing the LSM6DS33 datasheet. parts_sheet.json row R8.04 (the cited high-performance-mode current) gives value 1.25 with unit 'mA', not 'mW'. The revision is not fully consistent with the design it changes: design/nodes/firmware.balance_task.json's "sample_rate" quantity was rewritten from {unit: Hz, value: 100} to {unit: ms, value: 2.5}, switching physical kind from frequency to period while control.balance_loop.json and firmware.imu_driver.json keep "sample_rate" in Hz, a mismatch the base design did not have ([rule]); and electrical.imu.json's current_draw change (0.9->1.25 mA, rev 32) was followed up toward electrical.control_board but never toward control.balance_loop, which electrical.imu.json's own `constrains` list also names, with no no_change_justified entry added for that edge ([rule]).

design/nodes/firmware.balance_task.json's "sample_rate" quantity was rewritten from {unit: "Hz", value: 100} to {unit: "ms", value: 2.5} (diff hunk for firmware.balance_task.json; journal rev 30), switching the quantity's physical kind from frequency to period, while the sibling "sample_rate" quantities in control.balance_loop.json (400, Hz) and firmware.imu_driver.json (833, Hz) remain frequencies; the base design (rev 25) had all three in Hz, so this mismatch is newly introduced by the revision, not inherited.

design/nodes/control.balance_loop.json (journal.jsonl rev 29) writes torque_limit = {source: 'derived: [R1.18] * [R1.25]', unit: 'N*m', value: 0.32}. R1.18 = 0.16 kilogram_force*cm (parts_sheet.json), R1.25 = 2 (dimensionless) -> the cited arithmetic gives 0.32 kilogram_force*cm, which converts to about 0.0314 N*m (factor 0.0980665 kgf*cm->N*m), not the recorded 0.32 N*m -- roughly a 10x unit-conversion omission. The same node's own torque_peak quantity (unchanged by this revision) correctly applies that exact conversion: R1.07 (0.74 kgf*cm) * R1.25 (2) = 1.48 kgf*cm -> 0.145 N*m. The new torque_limit (0.32 N*m) is therefore both arithmetically wrong against its own cited source and physically backward -- larger than torque_peak even though it is derived from the smaller 'torque at max efficiency' figure rather than the larger 'stall torque' figure. The revision is therefore not consistent with the node's own established unit-conversion convention or with the rubric's unit-arithmetic requirement ([rule]).

control.balance_loop.torque_limit (journal.jsonl rev 29) is recorded as 0.32 N*m from 'derived: [R1.18] * [R1.25]' (0.16 kilogram_force*cm * 2 = 0.32 kilogram_force*cm), with the kgf*cm-to-N*m conversion omitted; properly converted it is about 0.0314 N*m. design/nodes/control.balance_loop.json (journal.jsonl line 29) adds speed_limit=513 rad/s sourced to https://www.pololu.com/product/3073/specs. parts_sheet.json rows R1.10 (650 rpm -> 68.1 rad/s, already recorded as no_load_speed in the same node) and R1.17 (490 rpm -> 51.3 rad/s) are the only speed-like rows on that page; neither converts to 513 rad/s. 513 is ~10x 51.3 (490*2*pi/6=513.1), and is ~7.5x the node's own no_load_speed (68.1 rad/s) and ~21.7x the wheel's actual no-load speed after the external 2.88:1 gearbox (68.1/2.88=23.6 rad/s, using control.balance_loop's own gear_ratio field). control.balance_loop.json's new speed_limit=513 rad/s does not match a correct rpm-to-rad/s conversion of any row on its cited source page (parts_sheet.json R1.10=650rpm->68.1 rad/s; R1.17=490rpm->51.3 rad/s); 513 is ~10x 51.3 rad/s (490*2*pi/6=513.1), the signature of an incorrect rpm-to-rad/s divisor. The revision records control.balance_loop.speed_limit=513 rad/s with source https://www.pololu.com/product/3073/specs (journal.jsonl line 29), implicitly claiming that figure is supported by that page. The revision is not internally consistent: electrical.motor_left's efficiency_point_output_power (design/nodes/electrical.motor_left.json, rev 29) carries unit 'J' while electrical.motor_right's identical, identically sourced quantity (rev 30) carries unit 'W'; the quantity is a power term in the input=output+heat balance that closes correctly in watts for motor_right but not for motor_left. design/nodes/electrical.motor_left.json (rev 29, written by this revision) records efficiency_point_output_power with unit 'J' and value 0.8, while electrical.motor_right.json (rev 30), citing the same source URL and the same value 0.8, records it with unit 'W'. Power and energy are different physical kinds (cross-domain standards §2); the quantity is required by its own name and by its role in the input/output/heat balance to be a power, so the 'J' unit on motor_left is a unit-consistency defect this revision introduced -- the field does not exist at all in the pre-revision journal entries (rev 11/12).

Redoing the declared balance by reading: electrical.motor_right closes exactly (2.52 W = 0.8 W + 1.72 W). electrical.motor_left's declared quantities do not close dimensionally: 2.52 W of input power cannot balance against 0.8 J (an energy) plus 1.72 W (a power) without an arbitrary time basis, so the balance the revision declares for motor_left does not close by reading.

electrical.control_board.json (worktree, rev 31) records sensor_power_draw as {source:'derived: [R8.03] * [R8.04]', unit:'W', value:4.13}; parts_sheet.json gives R8.03=3.3 V and R8.04=1.25 mA, so the arithmetic the source names yields 4.125 mW, not 4.125 W -- a 1000x unit error introduced by the revision (the prior rev 19 correctly used unit 'mW' for the equivalent figure). electrical.regulator_5v.json's no_change_justified for this same change reasons 'The sensor's rise of about 1.2 mW is negligible...', which only matches the correct mW-scale figure (4.13-2.97=1.16 mW) and directly contradicts the literal 4.13 W the revision actually wrote. electrical.control_board.json (worktree, journal rev 31) writes sensor_power_draw as {source:'derived: [R8.03] * [R8.04]', unit:'W', value:4.13}. parts_sheet.json gives R8.03 = {value:3.3, unit:'V'} and R8.04 = {value:1.25, unit:'mA'}. V x mA = mW, so the named arithmetic yields 4.125 mW, not 4.125 W -- the record's unit is wrong by a factor of 1000, and the prior revision (journal rev 19, same derived formula structure with R8.05) correctly used unit 'mW' for the equivalent figure. This is a unit/conversion-arithmetic error the revision itself introduced, judged normally (not exempted by 'conditions already in the design' since the base used the correct unit).

The follow-up chain is structurally present (firmware.imu_driver -> electrical.imu -> electrical.control_board -> electrical.regulator_5v's no_change_justified, and electrical.imu -> control.balance_loop's no_change_justified), but the reason electrical.regulator_5v.json gives ('The sensor's rise of about 1.2 mW is negligible against the regulator's 2 A rating') does not hold against the value electrical.control_board.json actually records (4.13 W, not 4.13 mW): a literal 4.13 W rise is not 'about 1.2 mW' and is not obviously negligible against a 2 A/10 W rail that also serves the MCU and other loads. control.balance_loop.json's no_change_justified text states 'The 100 Hz loop already exceeds the relaxed 50 Hz minimum,' but the design graph's own control.req_loop_rate.json (and journal rev 29) records the relaxed minimum as 5 Hz, not 50 Hz.
